title: Confirming candidate self-lensing binary detections with radial velocity measurements
summary: Compact objects in approximately edge-on binary orbits with stars are able to produce a self-lensing effect, amplifying light from their companion once per orbit. To date, five white dwarf self-lensing systems are known, while none are known containing black holes or neutron stars. Discovery of such systems is a potential method of finding quiescent black holes and neutron stars, most of which will be pristine and unchanged from their formation. Photometric detections can suffer from degeneracies in the lens mass and orbital parameters when the amplification and crossing time are not well constrained, while photometric searches produce too many false positives to allow radial velocity investigation of every candidate. Therefore we investigate the minimal radial velocity (RV) observational requirements to characterise such systems by simulating detectable self-lensing light curves, using those light curves to generate targeted RV observations, and fitting RV jointly with photometry. We evaluate the median relative error in the recovered lens mass and orbital period, alongside compact-object class recovery. We find that adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter error, with compact-object class generally easier to determine than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems, with even a small number of RV measurements resulting in substantial improvement in accuracy. These results suggest that multi-stage RV follow-up, starting with a small number of observations of many candidates, can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for further investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the minimal radial velocity (RV) follow-up needed to characterize self-lensing binary systems containing white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, showing that even a small number of RV measurements substantially improves lens-mass and orbital-period recovery and reliably classifies the compact object.
AI.motivation: Self-lensing in edge-on compact-object–star binaries is a promising route to discovering quiescent black holes and neutron stars, of which none are yet known (versus five white dwarf systems). Photometric detections alone suffer from degeneracies between lens mass and orbital parameters and generate too many false positives to permit RV follow-up of every candidate, so the required RV investment must be established.
AI.method: The authors simulate detectable self-lensing light curves, use them to generate targeted RV observation schedules, and perform joint fitting of RV data with photometry. They then measure the median relative error in recovered lens mass and orbital period, along with compact-object class recovery, as a function of the number and precision of RV measurements.
AI.result: Adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter errors. Compact-object class is generally easier to recover than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by the number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems; even a small number of RV measurements yields substantial improvement.
AI.conclusion: A multi-stage RV follow-up strategy—beginning with a small number of observations across many candidates—can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for deeper investigation.

title: Analog Electronic Computation of Stellar Structure: Polytropic Benchmarks, Circuit Scaling, and Error-Controlled Verification
summary: We present an electronic analog-computing framework for static stellar-structure equations and verify it using polytropic Lane-Emden benchmarks with known or high-accuracy reference solutions. Starting from an exploratory operational-amplifier and multiplier circuit, we identify sign, coefficient, central-regularity, and signal-conditioning problems that complicate direct electronic implementation. We develop dimensionless first-order formulations, derive regular finite-radius initial conditions, and construct voltage-scaled analog architectures with controlled signal headroom. The principal formulation uses a positive derivative state and reproduces the surface locations and dimensionless mass coefficients of the n = 0, 1, and 3 polytropes at the ideal scaled-voltage level. A common circuit architecture accommodates all three benchmarks, while the nonlinear n = 3 case demonstrates how voltage scaling and computation-speed adjustments can preserve the governing equations. Sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations quantify the propagation of calibration uncertainties into stellar observables. A separate regularized n = 1 circuit, implemented using AD734 and OPAx197 vendor macromodels, passes all 67 deterministic certification cases and three independently seeded Monte Carlo populations of 1000 cases each. All cases satisfy the predefined first-zero error tolerance of 0.020, with no saturation or convergence failures. A stricter 0.1% accuracy threshold is reported for characterization but is not used as the certification criterion. We also demonstrate a dimensionless four-state radiative extension beyond polytropic models. The results establish a reproducible framework for analog computation of stellar-structure benchmarks while explicitly distinguishing ideal calculations, vendor-macromodel verification, and future physical-hardware validation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an electronic analog-computing framework for static stellar-structure equations, validated against polytropic Lane–Emden benchmarks using dimensionless first-order formulations, regular finite-radius initial conditions, and voltage-scaled analog architectures, with sensitivity/Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification and vendor-macromodel verification.
AI.motivation: Direct electronic implementation of stellar-structure equations is complicated by sign, coefficient, central-regularity, and signal-conditioning problems; the work aims to establish a reproducible analog-computation framework for stellar-structure benchmarks.
AI.method: Develops dimensionless first-order formulations with derived regular finite-radius initial conditions and voltage-scaled analog architectures with controlled signal headroom; the principal formulation uses a positive derivative state. A common circuit accommodates n = 0, 1, 3 polytropes; sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations propagate calibration uncertainties; a regularized n = 1 circuit is verified with AD734 and OPAx197 vendor macromodels across 67 deterministic cases and three Monte Carlo populations of 1000.
AI.result: The principal formulation reproduces surface locations and dimensionless mass coefficients of the n = 0, 1, 3 polytropes at the ideal scaled-voltage level; the n = 3 case shows voltage scaling and computation-speed adjustments preserve the governing equations. The regularized n = 1 circuit passes all 67 deterministic certification cases and three 1000-case Monte Carlo populations under a first-zero error tolerance of 0.020, with no saturation or convergence failures; a stricter 0.1% threshold is reported only for characterization.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a reproducible framework for analog computation of stellar-structure benchmarks, explicitly distinguishing ideal calculations, vendor-macromodel verification, and future physical-hardware validation, and demonstrates a dimensionless four-state radiative extension beyond polytropic models.

title: Charting the Galactic Underworld II: Strategies for Identifying BHs and NSs with LISA
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, submitted to AAS journals - comments welcome!
summary: Stellar-mass black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs) observed by space-based gravitational-wave detectors offer constraints on binary stellar evolution that are complementary to those from ground- based detectors. The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to detect hundreds of double compact objects (DCOs) containing a BH or NS, but distinguishing these sources from the far more numerous double white dwarfs (WDWDs) may prove challenging. We use adaptive importance sampling with COSMIC to synthesise large populations of BHBH, BHNS, NSNS, BHWD, and NSWD binaries. We combine these binaries with a Milky Way star-formation history and integrate their Galactic orbits with cogsworth, repeating our simulations for a grid of variations in uncertain (binary) stellar physics. We find that LISA detections are largely insensitive to the changes in Galactic position resulting from natal kicks. We then assess how well chirp mass, eccentricity, distance from the Galactic plane, and orbital frequency distinguish BH- and NS-hosting DCOs from WDWDs, accounting for LISA measurement uncertainties. Using chirp mass alone distinguishes only 50-60% of BHBHs and BHNSs, and ~40% of NSNSs, but combining this with orbital frequency recovers 90-100% of BHBHs and BHNSs and around ~50% of NSNSs, with eccentricity further improving the recovery of NSNSs to around 60-70%. Distance from the Galactic plane adds little discriminating power, though it can recover a handful of NSWDs that are missed otherwise. These methods will help identify a significantly larger number of BHs and NSs in LISA data that would be missed by a chirp mass cut alone.

AI.tldr: LISA will detect hundreds of BH/NS double compact objects mixed with far more numerous double white dwarfs; combining chirp mass, orbital frequency, and eccentricity recovers 90-100% of BH/NS binaries that a chirp-mass cut alone would miss.
AI.motivation: Space-based detectors like LISA can constrain binary stellar evolution complementarily to ground-based detectors, but separating the hundreds of BH- and NS-hosting double compact objects from the much larger population of double white dwarfs (WDWDs) is challenging. A simple chirp-mass selection is insufficient, so better discriminants are needed.
AI.method: Adaptive importance sampling with COSMIC to synthesize large populations of BHBH, BHNS, NSNS, BHWD, and NSWD binaries; combine these with a Milky Way star-formation history; integrate Galactic orbits with cogsworth; repeat over a grid of variations in uncertain binary stellar physics. Then assess how chirp mass, eccentricity, distance from the Galactic plane, and orbital frequency separate BH/NS-hosting DCOs from WDWDs, accounting for LISA measurement uncertainties.
AI.result: LISA detections are largely insensitive to changes in Galactic position from natal kicks. Chirp mass alone distinguishes only 50-60% of BHBHs and BHNSs and ~40% of NSNSs. Adding orbital frequency recovers 90-100% of BHBHs and BHNSs and ~50% of NSNSs; eccentricity further raises NSNS recovery to ~60-70%. Distance from the Galactic plane adds little discriminating power but recovers a handful of NSWDs otherwise missed.
AI.conclusion: Multi-parameter classification (chirp mass + orbital frequency + eccentricity) substantially outperforms a chirp-mass-only cut, enabling identification of significantly more BHs and NSs in LISA data.

title: AGB-star Mass Transfer Products in Stellar Streams as Tracers of Density in Dissolved Star Clusters
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: The least dense globular clusters (GCs) appear to host the highest fractions of stars with chemical signatures of mass transfer from asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companions. Recent observations suggest the fraction may be even higher in stellar streams that are debris of tidally disrupted (preferentially low-density) GCs. We explore whether this is attributable to lower encounter rates in less-dense GCs allowing more of the relevant binaries to survive dynamical hardening, or outright disruption, long enough to undergo AGB mass transfer. We run a small suite of GC simulations varying initial density using the code CMC with its latest observationally motivated binary prescriptions. Using CMC's built-in COSMIC code for binary stellar evolution, we first identify primordial binaries that would, if left unperturbed, likely undergo AGB mass transfer via either standard or wind Roche-lobe overflow. We then check how many of those binaries survive GC dynamics in CMC long enough to experience AGB mass transfer. We find that wind Roche-lobe overflow is necessary to reproduce the fraction of (sub)giant stars in Galactic GCs that are likely products of AGB mass transfer (~1%) and that binary dynamics plausibly explain why this fraction appears lower in dense, intact GCs than stellar streams. The abundance of mass-transfer products (also collision products and binaries) in upcoming surveys of stellar streams without known progenitors will thus probe the densities of dissolved GCs---difficult to determine otherwise but key to improved stream modeling and predicted rates of many astrophysical transients.

AI.tldr: Binary dynamics in globular clusters (GCs) can explain why the fraction of stars showing AGB mass-transfer chemical signatures is higher in low-density GCs and stellar streams than in dense, intact GCs; wind Roche-lobe overflow (wind RLOF) is required to reproduce the observed ~1% fraction of such (sub)giant stars.
AI.motivation: Observations show that the least dense GCs host the highest fractions of stars with chemical signatures of mass transfer from AGB companions, and the fraction may be even higher in stellar streams that are debris of tidally disrupted, preferentially low-density GCs. The authors ask whether this trend arises because lower encounter rates in less-dense GCs allow more of the relevant binaries to survive dynamical hardening or disruption long enough to undergo AGB mass transfer.
AI.method: The authors run a small suite of GC simulations with the CMC code, varying the initial density and adopting its latest observationally motivated binary prescriptions. Using CMC's built-in COSMIC binary stellar evolution code, they first identify primordial binaries that, if unperturbed, would likely undergo AGB mass transfer via either standard Roche-lobe overflow or wind RLOF, then track how many of these binaries survive GC dynamics long enough to experience AGB mass transfer.
AI.result: Wind RLOF is necessary to reproduce the ~1% fraction of (sub)giant stars in Galactic GCs that are likely products of AGB mass transfer, and binary dynamics plausibly explain why this fraction appears lower in dense, intact GCs than in stellar streams.
AI.conclusion: The abundance of mass-transfer products—along with collision products and binaries—in upcoming surveys of stellar streams with unknown progenitors will probe the densities of dissolved GCs, which are otherwise difficult to determine but key to improved stream modeling and predicted rates of many astrophysical transients.

title: Solar Photospheric Flows and the Origin of Active Regions
summary: The early evolutionary stages of some active regions (ARs) are analysed with the aim of resolving one of the paramount-importance problems of heliophysics: what plays a primary, active role in the formation of active regions and sunspots---magnetic fields or motion of solar plasma? In particular, the first view underlies the popular model of rising $Ω$-shaped, twisted flux-tube loop of strong magnetic field. In this study, optical images obtained by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) of the Solar Dynamics Observatory are used along with full-vector maps of magnetic field based on HMI data. Maps of fluid-particle tracks are constructed using local correlation tracking of photospheric brightness elements. Comparisons of optical and magnetic maps for three developing active regions confirm the conclusion made by Bumba and Howard in the mid-1960s that the supergranulation pattern is not destroyed by the emerging magnetic field of the developing AR, which would be inevitable if a loop of the strong-magnetic-field flux tube rose through the subphotospheric layers. There are no signs of spreading flows on scales comparable to the size of the whole active region. Various forms of dissymmetry between the leading and trailing parts of ARs are revealed. Next, an example of a well-developed sunspot group is considered, which demonstrates that the twist of the magnetic configuration may develop much later than the group starts growing. It is concluded that plasma flows appear to be determinant with respect to magnetic fields. The considered scenarios of the origin of ARs are in sharp contradiction with the rising-tube model.

AI.tldr: Optical and full-vector magnetic HMI observations of developing active regions show that supergranulation persists through flux emergence and no AR-scale spreading flows or flux-tube signatures appear, indicating plasma flows are the primary/determining agent rather than rising strong-field flux tubes.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a central heliophysics question: whether magnetic fields or plasma motions play the primary, active role in forming active regions (ARs) and sunspots. The dominant rising Ω-shaped twisted flux-tube model assumes strong magnetic fields lead emergence; the authors test this against observations of early AR evolution.
AI.method: Early evolutionary stages of developing ARs are analyzed using SDO/HMI optical images plus HMI-based full-vector magnetic field maps. Fluid-particle track maps are derived via local correlation tracking (LCT) of photospheric brightness elements, allowing direct comparison of optical (granulation/supergranulation) and magnetic structures. Three developing ARs are examined, plus one well-developed sunspot group.
AI.result: Comparisons confirm Bumba & Howard's mid-1960s finding that the supergranulation pattern is not destroyed by emerging AR magnetic fields—an outcome inevitable if a strong-field flux-tube loop rose through subphotospheric layers. No spreading flows on scales comparable to the whole AR are detected. Various forms of lead–trail (leading/trailing) dissymmetry are revealed. In a well-developed sunspot group, magnetic-configuration twist develops much later than the onset of group growth.
AI.conclusion: Plasma flows appear to be determinant with respect to magnetic fields. The observed AR formation scenarios are in sharp contradiction with the rising-tube model, supporting flow-driven rather than field-driven origin of ARs and sunspots.

title: Detection of Solar-like Oscillations and Granulation at Infrared Wavelengths using JWST
comment: Recently resubmitted to APJLetters following favourable referee report
summary: Stellar oscillations and granulation are key probes of stellar convection, one of the most poorly understood processes in stars. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation, but hitherto both processes have only been measured at optical wavelengths. Here we present the first detection of oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 that were obtained to study the atmosphere of an exoplanet. We find that the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but with a functional form that deviates from simple blackbody scaling. The detection opens the door to detailed tests of 3D convection models, facilitates the combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands for exoplanet observations, and supports the predicted asteroseismic yields from the infrared time-domain data that will soon be obtained by the Roman Space Telescope.

AI.tldr: First detection of stellar oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V star WASP-121, showing amplitudes decrease with wavelength in a manner that deviates from simple blackbody scaling.
AI.motivation: Stellar oscillations and granulation probe convection, a poorly understood process. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of their amplitudes, yet both have so far been measured only at optical wavelengths, leaving these predictions untested.
AI.method: Analysis of JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121, originally taken to study an exoplanet atmosphere, to detect and measure oscillation and granulation amplitudes in infrared passbands.
AI.result: Both oscillation and granulation amplitudes are detected in the infrared and decrease with wavelength, qualitatively consistent with expectations, but their functional form deviates from simple blackbody scaling.
AI.conclusion: The detection enables detailed tests of 3D convection models, supports joint modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands, and underpins predicted asteroseismic yields from future Roman Space Telescope infrared time-domain data.

title: Distinct stellar-parameter dependencies of granulation and mesogranulation in red giants
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables, including appendix. Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Granulation and mesogranulation represent different spatial and temporal scales of convection, but are commonly assumed to follow the same stellar atmospheric scaling relations in red giants. We test this assumption using the largest sample assembled for this purpose to date -- 9,328 Kepler red giants spanning the red giant branch and red clump phase, cross-matched with APOGEE stellar parameters. We model each star's power spectrum background to obtain the radius-corrected amplitude and characteristic frequency of both components, and derive empirical scaling relations with effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity through Bayesian model comparison. Gaussian Process and symbolic regression provide independent validation. We find that granulation and mesogranulation are not self-similar: their surface-gravity dependencies are statistically indistinguishable, consistent with a shared envelope geometry, but their temperature dependencies diverge: mesogranulation's amplitude rises steeply with Teff, whereas granulation's shows no statistically justified dependence, and both frequencies respond weakly and similarly. We propose that this pattern is consistent with granulation forming in a thin near-surface layer, where radiation takes over from convection and the Mach number depends only weakly on Teff. Mesogranulation originates deeper, where convection carries the full flux and its Mach number and cell size increase with Teff. Metallicity raises both amplitudes but has little effect on the frequencies. Our results indicate that the self-similarity assumption underlying two-component background models does not hold, with direct implications for background modeling and its downstream application in Galactic archaeology.

AI.tldr: Using 9,328 Kepler red giants cross-matched with APOGEE, the authors show that granulation and mesogranulation do NOT follow the same atmospheric scaling relations: gravity dependence is shared, but temperature dependence diverges, refuting the self-similarity assumption of two-component background models.
AI.motivation: Two-component background models for red giants assume granulation and mesogranulation obey the same stellar atmospheric scaling relations, but this self-similarity assumption had never been rigorously tested on a large, homogeneous sample.
AI.method: Largest sample to date: 9,328 Kepler red giants (RGB + red clump) cross-matched with APOGEE stellar parameters. Each star's power-spectrum background was modeled to extract radius-corrected amplitude and characteristic frequency of both components; empirical scaling relations with Teff, log g, and metallicity were derived via Bayesian model comparison, independently validated with Gaussian Processes and symbolic regression.
AI.result: Granulation and mesogranulation are not self-similar. Their log g dependencies are statistically indistinguishable (shared envelope geometry), but temperature dependencies diverge: mesogranulation amplitude rises steeply with Teff, while granulation amplitude shows no statistically justified Teff dependence; both frequencies respond weakly and similarly. Metallicity raises both amplitudes but barely affects frequencies.
AI.conclusion: The self-similarity assumption underlying two-component background models is invalid. This is interpreted physically: granulation forms in a thin near-surface layer (radiation-dominated, weak Mach-number dependence on Teff), whereas mesogranulation originates deeper (convection carries full flux, Mach number and cell size increase with Teff). Implications extend to background modeling and downstream Galactic archaeology applications.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS survey: A Keplerian Circumbinary Disk Candidate in the High-mass Star-forming Region IRAS 08303-4303
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present the ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations of IRAS 08303-4303, a high-mass star-forming region, with an angular resolution of $\sim 0.3''$ ($\sim 700$ au at the distance of 2.35 kpc). Six dense condensations are identified in the 1.3 mm continuum, and at least four of them are associated with molecular outflows. The estimated outflow parameters, particularly mass outflow rates $\geq 10^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, suggest that the driving sources are high-mass young stellar objects. Two of the condensations are forming a wide protobinary system with a separation of $\sim 900$ au. They reside within a single rotating structure, identified as a circumbinary disk which has a mass of about 2 $M_{\odot}$. This structure is traced by multiple molecular lines and exhibits a Keplerian rotation pattern. Based on the Keplerian rotation assumption, the enclosed mass is derived to be between 32 and 61 $M_{\odot}$: 22-43 $M_{\odot}$ for the primary and 10-18 $M_{\odot}$ for the secondary. The circumbinary disk is on the whole gravitationally stable, yet some parts with Toomre $Q < 2$ indicate potential fragmentation. Various molecular lines reveal a streamer-like structure connecting to the circumbinary disk, suggesting transfer of material from the envelope to the protobinary system through it. Despite the observational rarity of such circumbinary disks around high-mass YSOs, the high binary fraction among massive stars underscores their significance. This source, therefore, serves as a key laboratory for understanding the formation of high-mass binary systems.

AI.tldr: ALMA 1.3 mm observations of IRAS 08303-4303 resolve six dense condensations, at least four driving molecular outflows, and reveal a ~2 Msun Keplerian circumbinary disk hosting a wide ~900 au high-mass protobinary (32-61 Msun total), indicating envelope-to-system mass transfer via a streamer.
AI.motivation: Circumbinary disks around high-mass young stellar objects are observationally rare, yet the high binary fraction among massive stars makes them crucial for understanding high-mass binary formation. IRAS 08303-4303 is presented as a key laboratory to study this process.
AI.method: ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations at ~0.3'' (~700 au) resolution; identification of dense condensations in 1.3 mm continuum; outflow parameter estimation; kinematic analysis of multiple molecular lines to detect Keplerian rotation and derive enclosed masses; Toomre Q stability assessment; streamer identification.
AI.result: Six dense condensations detected, at least four with molecular outflows and mass outflow rates >=1e-4 Msun/yr, implying high-mass YSOs. Two condensations form a wide protobinary (~900 au separation) within a single ~2 Msun rotating circumbinary disk exhibiting Keplerian rotation. Derived enclosed mass is 32-61 Msun (primary 22-43 Msun, secondary 10-18 Msun). The disk is largely gravitationally stable but has regions with Toomre Q<2 indicating potential fragmentation. A streamer-like structure connects the envelope to the disk.
AI.conclusion: IRAS 08303-4303 hosts a rare circumbinary disk around a high-mass protobinary, with material fed from the envelope via a streamer and some fragmentation potential. It provides a valuable laboratory for understanding high-mass binary formation.

title: A precise TESS ephemeris for the short-period binary TIC-259864042
summary: This paper presents a precise eclipse-timing analysis of TIC 259864042 (= EC 02406--6408, Gaia DR3 4647004122914240640) using eleven sectors of TESS photometry spanning 2018--2025 (7.1 yr). The system exhibits a single deep eclipse with a V-shaped profile at phase 0 and no detectable counterpart at phase 0.5. Four independent period-search methods converge to a common period agreeing to within 7 parts per million. An independent reduction with the SHERLOCK pipeline, using its own 120-second TESS photometry, confirms the same period at the same precision. A joint linear ephemeris fit gives P = 0.46048676 $\pm$ 0.0000001 d (11.059 h) and T_0 = 2458325.70381 $\pm$ 0.00002 BJD, with a residual RMS of 0.87 min across the 7.1-yr baseline. Per-sector ephemeris fits show residual medians within $\pm$0.42 min of zero, confirming that no cycle slip has occurred across the large TESS data gaps. The period is stable at the level of $Δ$BIC = +5.21 (in favour of the constant-period model); an upper limit of $|\dot{P}| \le 1 \times 10^{-9}$ d d$^{-1}$ is placed on any secular period change. A PHOEBE 2.4 fit to the Sector 27 light curve yields $i = 80.8^{\circ} \pm 0.5^{\circ}$, $R_1 = 0.21 \pm 0.01\ R_{\odot}$, $R_2 = 0.25 \pm 0.02\ R_{\odot}$, $q = 0.49 \pm 0.07$, consistent with a grazing detached geometry and a mid-M-dwarf companion. The TESS light curve alone cannot distinguish between the two temperatures 25100 K and 31000 K. The paper discusses the system in the context of the sdB eclipsing binary population, and notes that while the current data are consistent with a short-period sdB+M-dwarf architecture, a phase-resolved spectrum is needed to independently confirm the sdB identification.

AI.tldr: A 7.1-yr TESS eclipse-timing analysis of TIC 259864042 yields a highly precise, stable period of 0.46048676 d; PHOEBE fitting supports a grazing detached sdB + mid-M-dwarf geometry, pending spectroscopic confirmation.
AI.motivation: The system is a candidate short-period sdB eclipsing binary, a class where precise eclipse timing can constrain binary architecture and test for orbital period changes; existing data lack a precise, long-baseline ephemeris and a quantitative geometric solution.
AI.method: Eleven TESS sectors (2018-2025, 7.1 yr, 120-s photometry) were analyzed with four independent period-search methods, cross-checked by the SHERLOCK pipeline; a joint linear ephemeris fit, per-sector residual analysis, a BIC-based constant-vs.-varying period test, and a PHOEBE 2.4 fit to the Sector 27 light curve were performed.
AI.result: P = 0.46048676 ± 0.0000001 d (11.059 h), T0 = 2458325.70381 ± 0.00002 BJD, residual RMS 0.87 min; per-sector medians within ±0.42 min; ΔBIC = +5.21 favoring a constant period with |Pdot| ≤ 1e-9 d/d. PHOEBE gives i = 80.8° ± 0.5°, R1 = 0.21 ± 0.01 Rsun, R2 = 0.25 ± 0.02 Rsun, q = 0.49 ± 0.07; photometry alone cannot discriminate 25100 K vs 31000 K.
AI.conclusion: The data are consistent with a stable, short-period grazing detached sdB + mid-M-dwarf binary, but a phase-resolved spectrum is required to independently confirm the sdB identification and resolve the primary temperature.

title: Eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We have identified numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triple star systems from observations made with the space telescope TESS. For many of these systems we can potentially determine their dynamical and astrophysical parameters with high precision, in some cases even without the use of radial velocity data. In the present paper we report the comprehensive study of eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems, taken from this larger sample: TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, 385933895. Besides the photometric data from the TESS observations, we obtained supplementary ground-based photometric measurements, as well as radial velocity measurements for some of the systems. The eclipse timing variation curves extracted from the TESS data and from the ground-based follow up data, the photometric light curves, radial velocity data, and the spectral energy distribution are combined in a complex photodynamical analysis to yield the stellar and orbital parameters for all of the investigated systems. The outer periods are in the range of 63-294 days, including the currently sixth tightest known triple system, TI 385933895 with an outer to inner period ratio of 9.82. We find that all of the triples are nearly coplanar, with mutual inclination angles of <=2.5deg. Despite such flatness, we still detect eclipse depth variations in TIC 220456364 that are induced by orbital plane precession. Moreover, we find that TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple system. Finally we make some statistical assessments of a number of the orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances of these systems.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive photodynamical study of eight new triply eclipsing hierarchical triple systems identified with TESS, deriving precise stellar and orbital parameters and characterizing their architecture.
AI.motivation: TESS has enabled the identification of numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triple systems whose dynamical and astrophysical parameters can potentially be determined with high precision, sometimes without radial velocity data. This motivates a detailed, multi-source analysis of a subsample of new systems.
AI.method: Combined TESS photometry with ground-based follow-up photometry, radial velocity measurements (for some systems), eclipse timing variation curves, light curves, and spectral energy distributions in a complex photodynamical analysis to yield stellar and orbital parameters for all eight systems (TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, 385933895).
AI.result: Outer periods span 63-294 days; the sample includes the sixth tightest known triple system, TIC 385933895, with an outer-to-inner period ratio of 9.82. All triples are nearly coplanar with mutual inclinations <=2.5 deg. Despite this flatness, eclipse depth variations induced by orbital plane precession are detected in TIC 220456364. TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple system. Statistical assessments of orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances are provided.
AI.conclusion: The eight systems are confirmed as triply eclipsing hierarchical triples (one likely a quadruple), with nearly coplanar orbits, precise parameters derivable via photodynamical modeling, and a notable precession signal and record-tight configuration, providing a valuable sample for statistical characterization of such systems.

title: Analysis of a coronal hole jet in the chromosphere and the transition region with IRIS data and SDO observations
comment: accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Coronal jets are transient phenomena that occur throughout the solar atmosphere, often triggered by the activation of mini-filaments. Jets are an important field of study, as they are believed to contribute to the mass supply of the solar wind. We study a small-scale solar jet occurring in a low-latitude coronal hole, focusing on traces of the jet eruption to the lower atmosphere, utilizing chromospheric and transition region diagnostics. We also investigate the possible mechanisms and dynamic conditions leading to its onset. We analyze ultraviolet spectra from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph to investigate chromospheric dynamics and their connection to the transition region, using diagnostics of the Mg II k 2796.35 Å and Si IV 1393.75 Å lines, together with non-LTE inversions. We complement this analysis with multiwavelength imaging and magnetograms from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, as well as magnetic field modeling. The analysis of Mg II k and Si IV parameters reveals a coupling between chromospheric and transition region plasma dynamics. Profiles on the jet spire present deeper central reversals, larger peak separations and higher transition region Doppler velocities. The jet initiation is associated with a mini-filament-like structure, preceded by dynamic variations in the photospheric magnetic field. We find single-peaked Mg II k profiles at one of its footpoints, possibly indicating plasma drainage. The presence of a null point and a quasi-separatrix layer suggests that reconnection can play a role in the mini-filament-like structure destabilization and jet eruption. This study suggests that the signature and possibly the origin of coronal jets can be traced down to the chromosphere. The detailed analysis of the Mg II k profiles at the jet spire and the mini-filament-like structure may provide valuable observational constraints for future MHD simulations.

AI.tldr: A small-scale coronal jet in a low-latitude coronal hole is traced down to the chromosphere and transition region, linking mini-filament destabilization and magnetic reconnection (null point, QSL) to jet eruption and plasma drainage.
AI.motivation: Coronal jets are transient events thought to contribute to solar wind mass supply, but their lower-atmospheric signatures and onset conditions remain poorly constrained observationally.
AI.method: IRIS UV spectra analyzed via Mg II k 2796.35 Å and Si IV 1393.75 Å diagnostics plus non-LTE inversions; complemented by SDO multiwavelength imaging, magnetograms, and magnetic field modeling.
AI.result: Mg II k and Si IV parameters show chromosphere–transition region coupling; the jet spire exhibits deeper central reversals, larger peak separations, and higher TR Doppler velocities. Jet initiation is associated with a mini-filament-like structure preceded by photospheric magnetic field variations; a single-peaked Mg II k profile at one footpoint suggests plasma drainage; a null point and quasi-separatrix layer indicate reconnection-driven destabilization.
AI.conclusion: Jet signatures and possibly their origin can be traced to the chromosphere; Mg II k profiles at the spire and mini-filament-like structure provide observational constraints for future MHD simulations.

title: Unexpected Local Enhancement of Chromospheric Moreton Waves on the Sun
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ Letters
summary: Solar eruptions often drive shock waves. When propagating in the solar corona, strong shock waves would leave imprints on the solar surface in the chromosphere, which are called Moreton waves. Moreton waves generally decay as they move away. However, to our knowledge, for the first time we report that a Moreton wave is significantly enhanced midway during propagation, as revealed by the spectroscopic observations from China's first solar satellite, the Chinese H$α$ Solar Explorer. Combining magnetic measurements from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we found that the location of the Moreton wave enhancement corresponds to a magnetic null point at an altitude of $\sim$70 Mm in the corona. It is demonstrated that the unexpected local enhancement of the Moreton wave is due to mode conversion around the magnetic null point, i.e., fast-mode waves are converted to slow-mode waves which are trapped locally. It is further revealed that, even for ordinary Moreton wave fronts, the H$α$ Doppler redshift velocity is positively correlated with the height of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points, implying that these low-lying null points, $\sim$1--7 Mm above the solar surface, facilitate mode conversion with different efficiency, thereby accounting for the spatially inhomogeneous Dopplergram of Moreton wave fronts.

AI.tldr: First reported observation of a Moreton wave significantly enhanced midway during propagation, attributed to fast-to-slow mode conversion at a coronal magnetic null point (~70 Mm altitude); widespread low-altitude null points also explain spatially inhomogeneous Doppler velocities in normal Moreton fronts.
AI.motivation: Moreton waves (chromospheric imprints of coronal shocks) are generally expected to decay as they propagate outward. The authors challenge this assumption by investigating an anomalous, locally enhanced Moreton wave, seeking to identify the physical mechanism responsible and to understand the spatial inhomogeneity of Moreton wave Doppler signatures.
AI.method: Spectroscopic observations from China's first solar satellite, the Chinese Hα Solar Explorer (CHASE), combined with magnetic field measurements from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The enhancement location was compared with the coronal magnetic topology, and Hα Doppler redshift velocities of the wave fronts were correlated with the heights of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points.
AI.result: The Moreton wave enhancement coincides spatially with a magnetic null point at ~70 Mm altitude in the corona. The local amplification is explained by mode conversion at the null point: fast-mode waves convert to slow-mode waves that become locally trapped. Additionally, the Hα Doppler redshift velocity of ordinary Moreton wave fronts is positively correlated with the height of widespread low-altitude null points (~1--7 Mm), indicating mode conversion with varying efficiency that produces the spatially inhomogeneous Dopplergram.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic null points play a key role in shaping Moreton wave morphology and kinematics through fast-to-slow mode conversion. Coronal null points can locally enhance Moreton waves rather than allowing monotonic decay, while low-lying null points modulate the Doppler signature of wave fronts, providing a unified explanation for both anomalous enhancement and spatial inhomogeneity.

title: Slow Massive-Star Formation and the O-Star ZAMS Deficit
summary: The scarcity of optically visible O stars near the theoretical zero-age main sequence (ZAMS) has puzzled astronomers for over four decades. We argue that it reflects prolonged accretion. If massive stars assemble over Myr timescales, as the inertial-inflow model predicts, core-hydrogen burning begins before accretion ends, and the stars become optically visible at the end of accretion on a birthline displaced from the standard ZAMS. We test this interpretation by comparing the hot-side envelope of Galactic O stars in the Kiel diagram with accreting stellar-evolution models, adopting a growth law $t_{\mathrm{form}}=τ_0(m_{\mathrm{f}}/60 M_\odot)^α$ with formation time $t_{\mathrm{form}}$ and final mass $m_{\mathrm{f}}$. The resulting birthlines reproduce both the displacement and the high-mass turnover of the observed envelope, with best-fitting parameters $(α,τ_0)=(0.52,4.3\,\mathrm{Myr})$, consistent with independent constraints from the luminosity functions of compact H II regions and OB stars. The two constraints have orthogonal degeneracy directions, so combining them narrows the allowed parameter space, yielding projected 90% confidence intervals $0.43<α<0.60$ and $3.9<τ_0/\mathrm{Myr}<5.0$. The inferred growth law agrees with cloud-scale simulations and the inertial-inflow model, and implies that mass assembly and main-sequence evolution overlap substantially in massive stars, with broader implications for stellar evolution and feedback.

AI.tldr: The absence of O stars near the ZAMS is explained by prolonged accretion: birthlines from accreting stellar-evolution models reproduce the observed Kiel-diagram envelope, yielding a growth law consistent with cloud-scale simulations.
AI.motivation: Optically visible O stars near the theoretical ZAMS are scarce, a puzzle persisting over four decades. The authors propose this reflects prolonged accretion, in which massive stars begin core hydrogen burning before accretion finishes if assembled over Myr timescales.
AI.method: The hot-side envelope of Galactic O stars in the Kiel diagram is compared with accreting stellar-evolution models using a growth law t_form = τ0 (m_f/60 M_sun)^α. The derived birthlines are fitted to the observed envelope, and combined with independent constraints from luminosity functions of compact H II regions and OB stars.
AI.result: Birthlines reproduce both the displacement and high-mass turnover of the observed envelope, with best-fit (α, τ0) = (0.52, 4.3 Myr). Combining orthogonal constraints from the two luminosity functions yields 90% confidence intervals 0.43 < α < 0.60 and 3.9 < τ0/Myr < 5.0.
AI.conclusion: The inferred growth law agrees with cloud-scale simulations and the inertial-inflow model, implying that mass assembly and main-sequence evolution overlap substantially in massive stars, with broad implications for stellar evolution and feedback.

title: Granulation-driven spectral irradiance variability of Sun-like stars
summary: Granulation,caused by convection in low-mass stars like the Sun, introduces small amplitude variations in the stellar brightness on timescales of minutes to hours. Often referred to as flicker or microvariability this signal can impede detecting Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars via stellar transits. Stellar flicker can also introduce uncertainties in determining stellar fundamental parameters and cause errors of up to 10% in the radius determination of transiting exoplanets. Both sources of uncertainties will propagate into planetary transmission spectra and resulting atmospheric retrievals. We present a method for modelling stellar flicker that enables scaling the flicker of Sun-like stars between different wavelengths and passbands to facilitate better solar-stellar comparisons. We use the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic code MURaM to simulate the granulation pattern on a Sun-like star and employ the radiative transfer code MPS-ATLAS for the spectral synthesis of the MURaM output, producing lightcurves of the granulation signal in various wavelengths and at different disc positions. Using these synthetic lightcurves, we establish scaling relations in the time and frequency domain between different wavelengths and passbands routinely used in stellar observations, such as the Kepler and TESS space telescopes. We find that the variability caused by granulation is very well correlated across wavelengths from 300 to 6000 nm, enabling scalings from one wavelength regime to another. We present the scaling sensitivities in different passbands and wavelength regimes that can be used to facilitate solar-stellar comparisons and help estimate stellar flicker in observations using photometric passbands and low-resolution transmission spectra.

AI.tldr: Granulation-driven flicker is modeled with MURaM + MPS-ATLAS to derive wavelength scaling relations that translate solar flicker across passbands (e.g., Kepler, TESS) for solar-stellar comparisons and noise estimation.
AI.motivation: Granulation causes minute-to-hour brightness variations (flicker/microvariability) that hamper transit detection of Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars, bias stellar parameter determination, and can produce up to 10% errors in transiting exoplanet radii. These uncertainties propagate into transmission spectra and atmospheric retrievals, motivating a way to compare and scale flicker between the Sun and other stars across wavelengths.
AI.method: 3D radiative MHD simulations with MURaM produce the granulation pattern of a Sun-like star; spectral synthesis with the MPS-ATLAS radiative transfer code converts the MURaM output into synthetic lightcurves of the granulation signal at multiple wavelengths and disc positions. Time- and frequency-domain scaling relations between wavelengths and commonly used photometric passbands (Kepler, TESS) are then derived.
AI.result: Granulation variability is very well correlated across wavelengths from 300 to 6000 nm, permitting scaling from one wavelength regime to another. Scaling sensitivities are obtained for several passbands and wavelength regimes.
AI.conclusion: The derived scaling relations enable solar-stellar comparisons and allow estimation of stellar flicker in observations using photometric passbands and low-resolution transmission spectra, supporting improved transit photometry and atmospheric retrieval.

title: Magnetic Activity as a Driver of Low-gravity-like Spectral Morphology in Late-M Dwarfs
summary: We present a systematic investigation of the connection between magnetic activity and the low-surface-gravity-like near-infrared spectral morphology of late-M dwarfs. Our sample includes TRAPPIST-1 observed with JWST NIRISS/SOSS and 22 late-M dwarfs observed with IRTF/SpeX, together with flare observations from K2, TESS, JWST NIRISS/SOSS, and literature-reported X-ray luminosities. Using one-component PHOENIX/NewEra spectral modeling, we find that all targets are better reproduced by lower-surface-gravity model spectra than by models with the expected high gravities of field late-M dwarfs. The retrieved surface gravities moderately correlate with independently measured gravity-sensitive spectral indices, with the strongest trends seen for FeH$_z$ at 0.998~$μ$m and FeH$_J$ at 1.2~$μ$m, both showing statistically significant Pearson and Spearman correlations with $p<0.005$. They also show strong anti-correlations with flare luminosity and X-ray luminosity: for both relations, Pearson and Spearman coefficients are $<-0.9$, with $p \leq 1.0\times10^{-4}$, indicating that more active stars tend to have spectra favoring lower-gravity morphologies. Time-series spectra of TRAPPIST-1 during two large flares show no clear short-timescale variations in selected photospheric indices, suggesting that persistent small-scale magnetic activity may play a more important role than large flares in modifying the photospheric temperature--pressure structure. A simplified radiative-transfer experiment further shows that activity-associated heating can produce lower-gravity-like spectral features even when the input surface gravity is fixed. Our results suggest that underestimated surface gravities in late-M dwarfs may reflect atmospheres modified by frequent, small-scale magnetic activity, such as microflares, producing emergent spectra that mimic lower-gravity morphology.

AI.tldr: Low-gravity-like NIR spectra of late-M dwarfs are shown to result from magnetic activity heating the atmosphere rather than from genuinely low surface gravity.
AI.motivation: Late-M dwarfs often yield underestimated surface gravities from spectral fitting, and the cause is unclear; the authors test whether magnetic activity drives the low-gravity-like near-infrared morphology.
AI.method: JWST NIRISS/SOSS spectrum of TRAPPIST-1 plus IRTF/SpeX spectra of 22 late-M dwarfs, combined with K2, TESS, JWST and X-ray flare/activity data. One-component PHOENIX/NewEra spectral fitting retrieves surface gravities, which are compared with gravity-sensitive indices (FeH_z 0.998 um, FeH_J 1.2 um) and activity measures; time-series spectra during two TRAPPIST-1 flares and a simplified radiative-transfer experiment test the mechanism.
AI.result: All targets are better fit by lower-gravity models. Retrieved gravity correlates moderately with FeH indices (p<0.005) and strongly anti-correlates with flare and X-ray luminosity (Pearson/Spearman <-0.9, p<=1e-4). No clear short-timescale index changes appear during large flares, while radiative-transfer tests reproduce low-gravity-like features with fixed input gravity under activity-associated heating.
AI.conclusion: Underestimated gravities in late-M dwarfs likely reflect atmospheres modified by persistent small-scale magnetic activity (e.g., microflares) that mimics low-gravity spectral morphology; large flares are not the dominant driver.
